questions.text: What does a production function describe?

options.a: The maximum feasible output from each input bundle.
options.b: The willingness to pay for inputs.
options.c: The firm's actual profit at every price.
options.d: The minimum consumer spending for any utility level.

questions.text: What is a production set?

options.a: Only the firm's profit-maximizing plans.
options.b: The set of bundles consumers prefer.
options.c: All technologically feasible input-output combinations.
options.d: Every market-clearing price vector.

questions.text: When is a production plan (x,y) technologically feasible if the production function is f(x)?

options.a: Whenever input spending equals revenue.
options.b: When y is no greater than f(x), assuming free disposal of output.
options.c: Only when y exceeds f(x).
options.d: Only when output price equals marginal cost.

questions.text: What are factors of production?

options.a: The prices of substitutes in consumption.
options.b: Only monetary profits.
options.c: Only finished goods sold to consumers.
options.d: Inputs such as labor, capital, land and raw materials.

questions.text: An isoquant depicts what?

options.a: Firms producing at identical average cost only.
options.b: Price and output combinations with equal profit.
options.c: Consumption bundles yielding equal utility.
options.d: Input combinations capable of producing a specified output level.

questions.text: Which feature distinguishes an isoquant from an indifference curve?

options.a: An isoquant relates physical inputs to output, while an indifference curve relates consumption bundles to utility.
options.b: Isoquants show fixed consumer income.
options.c: Isoquants are always upward sloping.
options.d: Indifference curves involve input prices.

questions.text: What does a higher isoquant usually represent under monotonic technology?

options.a: A lower amount of output.
options.b: A higher product price.
options.c: A higher level of achievable output.
options.d: The same output with a lower fixed cost only.

questions.text: In a Leontief or fixed-proportions production function, how are inputs related?

options.a: Firms can freely replace all inputs with any others.
options.b: They are always perfect substitutes.
options.c: One input always has zero marginal product.
options.d: They are perfect complements used in required proportions.

questions.text: What shape do fixed-proportions isoquants typically have?

options.a: Straight lines with constant negative slope.
options.b: Perfect circles.
options.c: Vertical lines at every output.
options.d: L-shaped with kinks at efficient input combinations.

questions.text: For f(x1,x2)=min(x1,x2), what happens if x1 increases while x2 remains strictly smaller?

options.a: Output necessarily doubles.
options.b: Output does not increase.
options.c: Output rises one-for-one.
options.d: Output decreases due to scale economies.

questions.text: With perfect-substitutes production technology, which form is typical?

options.a: f(x1,x2)=x1x2 only.
options.b: f(x1,x2)=min(a1x1,a2x2).
options.c: f(x1,x2)=max(0,x1-x2) necessarily.
options.d: f(x1,x2)=a1x1+a2x2 with positive coefficients.

questions.text: What shape are isoquants under perfect-substitutes technology with positive coefficients?

options.a: Convex parabolas opening upward.
options.b: L-shaped curves.
options.c: Straight lines.
options.d: Concentric circles.

questions.text: For a Cobb-Douglas production function A x1^a x2^b with positive exponents, what is generally true of isoquants in the positive quadrant?

options.a: They are straight lines for all a and b.
options.b: They must be L-shaped.
options.c: They slope downward and are smooth and convex to the origin.
options.d: They are horizontal at every output.

questions.text: How does the fixed-proportions technology differ from a perfect-substitutes technology?

options.a: Fixed proportions imply no need for both inputs.
options.b: Both allow the same flexible substitution.
options.c: Fixed proportions limit input substitution, while perfect substitutes permit constant-rate replacement.
options.d: Perfect substitutes require exact fixed input ratios.

questions.text: What does free disposal of inputs mean in production theory?

options.a: Extra inputs can be discarded without forcing output to fall.
options.b: The firm can acquire any input at zero price.
options.c: Extra output must always be sold at a profit.
options.d: Every input must have strictly increasing marginal product.

questions.text: What does monotonicity of the production function mean?

options.a: Adding inputs cannot reduce the maximum feasible output.
options.b: Adding inputs always doubles output.
options.c: Input prices rise whenever input quantity rises.
options.d: Average cost necessarily falls with output.

questions.text: If two input bundles can each produce at least y units, what does convexity of the input requirement set imply?

options.a: A weighted average necessarily produces less than y.
options.b: The input bundles must be identical.
options.c: Any weighted average of the two bundles can also produce at least y.
options.d: Each input must be a perfect substitute.

questions.text: Why is convexity economically useful in cost-minimization analysis?

options.a: It eliminates the role of input prices.
options.b: It supports well-behaved trade-offs and often interior or stable optimum input choices.
options.c: It forces all marginal products to be constant.
options.d: It guarantees every optimum uses only one factor.

questions.text: What is the marginal product of an input?

options.a: The cost of one more unit of output.
options.b: The additional output from a small increase in that input holding other inputs fixed.
options.c: Output divided by all input prices.
options.d: The additional revenue from an increase in market price.

questions.text: What is diminishing marginal product?

options.a: All factors have negative marginal products.
options.b: A doubling of all inputs yields less than double output by definition.
options.c: Total output necessarily declines as input use increases.
options.d: The marginal product of an input falls as more of that input is used, other inputs fixed.

questions.text: Why is diminishing marginal product different from decreasing returns to scale?

options.a: It changes one input holding others fixed, while returns to scale change all inputs proportionally.
options.b: Both definitions are identical.
options.c: Returns to scale concern only labor prices.
options.d: Diminishing marginal product requires output to be zero.

questions.text: What does the technical rate of substitution (TRS) describe?

options.a: How much of one input can be given up as another increases while holding output fixed.
options.b: The difference between accounting and economic profit.
options.c: The rate at which output price changes with consumer demand.
options.d: The willingness of a consumer to pay for insurance.

questions.text: For a differentiable two-input production function, what is the slope of an isoquant?

options.a: MP1+MP2.
options.b: -MP1/MP2.
options.c: MP2/MP1 always positive.
options.d: -w1/w2 regardless of the location on any isoquant.

questions.text: With a smoothly convex isoquant, what happens to the absolute slope as x1 increases along the isoquant?

options.a: It remains exactly fixed by definition of convexity.
options.b: It typically decreases.
options.c: It increases without bound.
options.d: It switches sign from negative to positive.

questions.text: What is the technical interpretation of a high absolute TRS of input 1 for input 2?

options.a: An additional unit of input 1 can replace relatively many units of input 2 at constant output.
options.b: Input 1 has no marginal product.
options.c: Input 2 must be free.
options.d: Input 1 cannot replace any input 2.

questions.text: At the kink of a Leontief isoquant, why is the standard smooth tangency condition inappropriate?

options.a: Both inputs always have identical prices.
options.b: The isoquant is not differentiable at the efficient input ratio.
options.c: Output is negative at the kink.
options.d: Production is impossible at the kink.

questions.text: What distinguishes the short run from the long run in production theory?

options.a: Short-run profits must equal zero.
options.b: In the long run all inputs are free.
options.c: Output cannot vary in the short run.
options.d: At least one input is fixed in the short run; all relevant inputs are variable in the long run.

questions.text: Why can a firm adjust more fully to a price or demand change in the long run?

options.a: It can vary inputs such as plant size that were fixed in the short run.
options.b: All consumer preferences become linear.
options.c: It never faces technological constraints in the long run.
options.d: Fixed costs rise with every output change by definition.

questions.text: What are constant returns to scale?

options.a: Scaling all inputs by t scales output by t, for t greater than zero.
options.b: Increasing one input by t always adds exactly t output.
options.c: Total cost is constant regardless of output.
options.d: Doubling all inputs always halves output.

questions.text: What are increasing returns to scale?

options.a: Doubling every input exactly doubles output.
options.b: Increasing one input at fixed others always produces more output.
options.c: Multiplying every input by t greater than one raises output by more than t.
options.d: All marginal products must increase at every bundle.

questions.text: What are decreasing returns to scale?

options.a: Marginal cost decreases at all output levels by definition.
options.b: Multiplying all inputs by t greater than one raises output by less than t.
options.c: Doubling inputs reduces output to zero.
options.d: Increasing one input must reduce total output.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas technology A x1^a x2^b, what determines returns to scale?

options.a: The level of the technology coefficient A only.
options.b: The sum of the exponents a+b.
options.c: The difference a-b only.
options.d: The ratio of factor prices only.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas technology with a+b=1, returns to scale are what?

options.a: Undefined regardless of inputs.
options.b: Decreasing.
options.c: Constant.
options.d: Increasing.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas technology with a+b>1, returns to scale are what?

options.a: Necessarily negative.
options.b: Constant.
options.c: Decreasing.
options.d: Increasing.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas technology with 0<a+b<1, returns to scale are what?

options.a: Constant.
options.b: Increasing.
options.c: Decreasing.
options.d: Necessarily zero output.

questions.text: A technology has diminishing marginal product of labor when capital is fixed. What can be inferred about returns to scale?

options.a: It must have constant returns to scale.
options.b: It must have decreasing returns to scale.
options.c: It must have increasing returns to scale.
options.d: Nothing definitive without knowing how output responds when all inputs change.

questions.text: What is a characteristic of perfect-substitutes production f=x1+2x2 under a common proportional scale-up?

options.a: It has decreasing returns to scale.
options.b: It has constant returns to scale.
options.c: It has increasing returns to scale.
options.d: Its returns to scale vary with prices.

questions.text: What is a characteristic of the Leontief production f=min(x1,2x2) under proportional scaling?

options.a: It has constant returns to scale.
options.b: It has no defined output.
options.c: It has decreasing returns to scale.
options.d: It has increasing returns to scale.

questions.text: When all inputs double and output triples, the observed response indicates what?

options.a: Constant returns to scale.
options.b: Increasing returns to scale over that change.
options.c: Diminishing marginal product of every input.
options.d: Decreasing returns to scale.

questions.text: When all inputs double and output rises by only 60%, the response indicates what?

options.a: Decreasing returns to scale over that change.
options.b: Negative marginal products of all inputs.
options.c: Increasing returns to scale.
options.d: Constant returns to scale.

questions.text: When input 2 is fixed, what does the slope of output against input 1 measure?

options.a: The marginal cost of output.
options.b: The rate of return on investment.
options.c: The marginal product of input 1.
options.d: The technical rate of substitution.

questions.text: What does a movement along one isoquant represent?

options.a: Changing the market price while input quantities stay fixed.
options.b: Increasing output by holding all inputs fixed.
options.c: Changes in consumer utility only.
options.d: Input substitution that leaves output unchanged.

questions.text: Why might one input's marginal product increase when the other input increases?

options.a: Returns to scale must be decreasing.
options.b: Diminishing marginal product forbids any complementarity.
options.c: An isoquant must always be upward sloping.
options.d: The inputs may be technologically complementary in raising each other's productivity.

questions.text: Which technological feature does the illustrated L-shaped isoquant capture?

options.a: Only one of the inputs is ever technologically productive.
options.b: Both inputs can replace each other at a constant rate.
options.c: Production requires inputs in fixed proportions at the efficient kink.
options.d: Output falls whenever a firm adds an input.
